Reading vs. Seeing

When we see something, we generally take it in all at once.

However, when we read, we typically read in a sequence, one word at a time. We could say that reading has a dimension of time (t).

Recurrent Neural Networks · Reading vs. Seeing04

Reading vs. Seeing

When we're looking at images, it doesn't really matter what image we saw previously.

However, as we read across time (t), what we've seen previously matters a LOT! It provides context to the token we're currently seeing.

Recurrent Neural Networks · Reading vs. Seeing05

Prediction in the Brain

Goldstein et al. (Nature Neuroscience, 2022) played a 30-minute podcast (5,113 words) and stopped before every word to ask people to guess it.

  • People guessed the next word right 28% of the time on average.
  • GPT-2's guesses lined up with theirs (correlation 0.79), and lined up better the more of the story GPT-2 could see, up to about 100 words back.
  • Electrodes on the brains of 9 epilepsy patients picked up signs of the upcoming word hundreds of milliseconds before it was heard, and a surprise signal after a word they didn't expect.

Our brains also predict the next word, and they need the context to do it.

Careful: matching a model's guesses says nothing about how the brain makes them. The brain is not an RNN.

Remembering Context

As we read through our input prompt over time (t) we need to remember, maintain, and build up the context of the sequence of embeddings we've seen so far.

\gold{h_t} = \tanh\bp{\gold{h_{t-1}}\,\Omega_h + \red{\text{Ɛ}_t}\,\Omega_x + b_h}
  • ht = context at time t (current timestep)
  • ht−1 = context from time t-1 (prior timestep)
  • Ɛt = embedding for current token
